messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
m=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor,\qquad A=m!.
\]

We want

\[
n\mid A^{n!}+450.
\]

Split the prime factors of \(n\) according to whether they divide \(A=m!\). Write

\[
n=uv,
\]

where every prime divisor of \(u\) is \(\le m\), and every prime divisor of \(v\) is \(>m\). Then \(\gcd(A,v)=1\).

### 1. Conditions on \(u\)

If \(p^e\mid u\), then \(p\le m\), so \(p\mid A\). Hence

\[
v_p(A^{n!})=n!\,v_p(A)\ge n!\ge e,
\]

so

\[
A^{n!}\equiv 0 \pmod{p^e}.
\]

Since \(n\mid A^{n!}+450\), we must have \(p^e\mid 450\). Therefore

\[
u\mid 450.
\]

### 2. Conditions on \(v\)

Since \(\gcd(A,v)=1\), Euler’s theorem applies. Also \(v\mid n\), so \(v\le n\), and thus \(\varphi(v)\le v-1\le n-1\). Therefore \(\varphi(v)\mid n!\), and

\[
A^{n!}\equiv 1 \pmod v.
\]

Thus

\[
1\equiv -450 \pmod v,
\]

so

\[
v\mid 451.
\]

Now

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2,\qquad 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

So \(u\mid 450\) and \(v\in\{1,11,41,451\}\).

Also, every prime divisor of \(v\) must be larger than \(m\).

---

### 3. Case analysis for \(v\)

#### Case \(v=1\)

Then \(n=u\le 450\). The value \(u=450\) works because

\[
\sqrt{450}<22,\qquad m=21,
\]

and all prime factors of \(450\) are \(\le 21\). So the largest in this case is \(450\).

#### Case \(v=11\)

We need \(11>m\), so \(m\le 10\). Hence

\[
n<11^2=121.
\]

Since \(n=11u\), we get \(u\le 10\). The largest divisor of \(450\) not exceeding \(10\) is \(10\), giving \(n=110\).

#### Case \(v=41\)

We need \(41>m\), so \(m\le 40\). Hence

\[
n<41^2=1681.
\]

Since \(n=41u\), we get \(u\le 40\). The largest divisor of \(450\) not exceeding \(40\) is \(30\), giving

\[
n=41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

This is valid because

\[
\sqrt{1230}<36,\qquad m=35,
\]

and \(35<41\), while all prime factors of \(30\) are \(\le 35\).

#### Case \(v=451\)

Then the smallest prime divisor of \(v\) is \(11\), so we would need \(m<11\), hence \(n<121\). But \(n\ge 451\), impossible.

---

Thus the largest possible value is \(1230\).

Indeed, for \(n=1230\), we have \(m=35\), and

\[
1230=30\cdot 41.
\]

Modulo \(30\), both \(35!\) and \(450\) are divisible by \(30\). Modulo \(41\), \(\gcd(35!,41)=1\), and \(40\mid 1230!\), so

\[
35!^{1230!}\equiv 1 \pmod{41}.
\]

Also \(450\equiv -1\pmod{41}\). Therefore

\[
35!^{1230!}+450\equiv 0 \pmod{41}.
\]

So \(1230\) indeed divides the expression.

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
